newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican military caught in new drug scandal.
newsitem.headline: Mexican military caught in new drug scandal.

text.p: The growing role of the military in Mexico's war on drugs came under fire on Monday after the armed forces admitted fresh cases of drug corruption in its ranks.

In a statement issued late on Sunday, the Defence Ministry said 34 military or ex-military personnel had been arrested this year "for their presumed responsibility in drug trafficking or for collaborating with it."

The admission followed a report in Mexico's news weekly Proceso that named generals and other top officers who in the last six years were allegedly given cars, pigs, farm machinery and other expensive gifts from drug lords.
It was a stunning revelation in a country where, until recently, even less was known about the secretive army's generals than the elusive drug capos they were supposed to be chasing.
Opposition legislators called for a full-scale probe, while some members of the Defence Committee lamented the damage that such revelations had done to army morale.
"It's a very delicate matter that needs a deep and rigorous investigation," Cuauhtemoc Sandoval, a high-ranking Party of the Democratic Revolution member of the committee, told Reuters.
"It's not right that the Mexican army is involved in actions against drug trafficking, because it runs the risk of ending up coopted and perverted by the (drug) mafias."

The army's anti-narcotics role has been stepped up since 1994, when President Ernesto Zedillo took office, and analysts said the new scandal highlighted the risks he is running in putting soldiers instead of police on the front line of the drug war.

"I never thought the military should be involved in the drugs war. This just illustrates that it opens up the institution to even more corruption than already existed," said Roderic Camp, professor of political science at Tulane University in New Orleans, who has written widely on the Mexican armed forces.
The allegations of corruption follow damaging charges against jailed Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, a top officer who headed the National Institute for Combatting Drugs.

He was denounced by fellow officers in February for allegedly receiving pay-offs from Mexico's late drug kingpin Amado Carrillo Fuentes. Gutierrez Rebollo is currently on trial and denies the charges against him.

The secret documents were leaked to Proceso during an army investigation against two officers -- one a colonel, the other a captain -- who allegedly were caught illegally copying them from computer disks for unspecified reasons. The two men were being held in a military jail.

In one case, they detailed the activities of retired Gen. Juan Felix Tapia Garcia, who the documents said was still working as an adviser to the military's high command. According to the documents, he was identified in 1991 "as partner and protector of Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, alias Don Neto," a well-known kingpin. He also received presents from other capos.
In its statement, the armed forces said all personnel mentioned in the documents no longer worked in the institution, and that some were under investigation.
